chapter_theme: The third ten, Palai Gauthamanar's songs for Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan: the king's sacrifices and open kitchen, the faults that block dharma's wheel, the bards he feeds in drought, the six-duty Brahmins whose word he follows, a series of enemy lands seen at their height and ruined by his anger, his own land watered even in drought, and the great rice offering before battle; the preface adds his conquests and his last journey to the forest.

21.reading: The poet praises the Chera who, guided by the five disciplines of the learned and speaking truth as clear as daybreak, keeps two fires going at once, the oblation of the sacrifice for the gods and the roaring kitchen where fat meat is fried without stint for every guest, so that both smells rise and please even the gods in the sky; he hails him as lord of the Puzhiyar whose cowherds find gems on the rocky pasture, shield of the Mazhavar and lord of the hill Ayirai, and wishes him, with his wife of fragrant hair and wandering rain-cool eyes, countless ages of life while the rains never fail.
21.nuance: Lines 7 and 13 call both fires ஆவுதி: the sacrificial ghee and the cooking fat of the guests' kitchen are the same kind of offering, and line 14 has them smell together (இரண்டு உடன் கமழும்). The poem ends not on the king's war but on his queen, a rare domestic close for a decade poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's sacrifices and open kitchen and blesses him and his queen

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the frying in the kitchen

22.reading: The poet tells Kuttuvan, descendant of rulers who kept away anger, desire, excessive indulgence, fear, lies, too much love and harsh punishment, the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, and so led an age when no one harmed or coveted, couples were not parted, food was shared and people died old and free of disease, that he who took the Kongar's land of cows and deep rock-cut wells and broke the guarded Agappa fort with its moat, walls and bow-engines has turned his anger on a festive watered country where men dam floods to the drum, so that, pitiably, it will become a great waste where at noon the jackal howls, the owl hoots and the demoness walks.
22.nuance: The list of faults in lines 1-4 is of excesses on both sides: harshness (தெறல் கடுமை) sits beside excessive kindness (கழிகண்ணோட்டம்) and excess of love, so the wheel of dharma is blocked by too much mercy as well as too little. The poem then praises the lineage for this restraint and ends with the king's anger laying a land waste; the poet's அளிய (pitiable) is his only comment.

thinai_evidence.note: because the king is angry with it, the rich enemy land will become waste

23.reading: The bards tell Kuttuvan of the golden garland, who even in a drought when cicadas cry on the dead unnam tree and the earth has lost its green ends the hunger of the street-singing musicians and throws great jewels even at small pleasures, that on their way to him they saw the lands of the kings who fought him and fled: once watered country of marutham trees, kaanchi-lined fords, fire-red murukku, conches, herons and lotus fields, they have become sky-high forest where grass blocks the untravelled roads and the wild cow lives happily with her bull.
23.nuance: The drought of lines 1-3 at home is answered by the king's giving, while the enemy's land, which had no drought, is ruined by war; the two halves weigh natural against man-made ruin. The wild cow living happily with her bull is the poem's sign that the forest has truly returned: pleasure has passed from people to beasts.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards report the rich lands of kings who fought him turned to forest

24.reading: The poet hails the leader of a great army whose warriors raise spears drawn from tiger-skin sheaths like spreading lightning, who conducts himself by the word of the Brahmins devoted to dharma who keep the six duties of learning, sacrificing, having others do both, giving and receiving, so that the world walks his way; husband of the queen of refined speech, he is harder to measure than the five elements, and the poet has seen his swelling wealth: an unfailing rice for all comers, pounded by pestles worn ringless, with meat cut by knives in the great pots, which all marvel at, so that even if the rain-cloud forgot its season when Venus stands to the north, his wealth would keep its yield.
24.nuance: The king's dharma is deference: he walks by the Brahmins' word and the world walks by his (lines 8-9). The closing claim that his wealth outlasts a failed monsoon makes royal plenty independent of the rain that the ethics books tie to just rule.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's conduct, measureless greatness and wealth

comparisons.tenor: the spears raised by the warriors
the king's greatness, harder to measure

25.reading: The poet tells the king that in the wide lands of others where he drove his tall chariot, its banners rippling like a waterfall off a mountain and its drum roaring like thunder, the fields trodden by his horses are no longer ploughed, the ground where his musth elephants spread knows no harvest, donkeys wander the commons his soldiers camped in, fire fanned by the wind has danced over the land, and the dried forest road where the owl-headed bird roams has become a great waste.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's invasion leaves others' lands ploughless and burned

26.reading: The poet says that in the land the king's warriors, like a Death that nothing afflicts, have raged against, where chariots spread no plough goes, where elephants trod no plough moves, and houses that echoed with churning hear no music, he grieves when he thinks of the wealth its old inhabitants knew: they, holding back tears and beating their hands, say the rain has failed and the heat has come and that this is the nature of the times, while their fenced homes turn to ruins overgrown with peerkku and nerunji and the old town loses its festivity.
26.nuance: The victims blame the season (காலையது பண்பு, line 7), not the king, while the poet knows the cause and says so in a praise poem; his நோகோ யானே is the most open grief for the conquered in the decade.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet grieves over the enemy land the king's warriors ravaged

27.reading: The poet tells the king that surely it is ruined, since he looked at it in anger: the desirable beauty of a good land of unfailing yield, where men wearing kuvalai and ambal and drinking toddy climb the marutham by the ford to dive, peacocks dance in the field groves when bangled women call, and carts sink in the mud of the neythal-lined fields so that the oxen strain, and no uproar was known but the shouting of the carters.
27.nuance: Only the first line tells of ruin; the other fifteen describe the land as it was, so the king's anger is measured by what it destroyed. The only 'uproar' of the old land is carts stuck in rich mud, the figure the next poem uses for the king's own country.

thinai_evidence.note: the beauty of the enemy's watered land is ruined by the king's angry look

28.reading: The poet says the king's wide land is rich indeed: since he guards it so well that his warriors, who broke the paired ranks of the enemy's elephants, forget their quick archery and the harvest never fails, even in a great drought when summer lingers, the hills turn pale and the falls run dry, the flood of the great river, crowned with straw, overflows its banks into the fields, and apart from the uproar of that red water no heat is known there.
28.nuance: The war is present only as something forgotten (கதழ்தொடை மறப்ப): peace at home is the warriors' idleness. Line 6 (நீணதொழில்) looks corrupt, so the cause clause is read loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's own land as safe and watered

29.reading: The poet says that the broad settlements, pitiably, used to flourish before the boundless army of Kuttuvan of many elephants spread over them, he whose fierce drum, fed with blood and mixed grain, calls him past the rules of battle to take hard forts: there bangled women rested their pestles against the plantains to pluck vallai, herons fat on ayirai fish crowded the trees above the ripe paddy and were chased off by the women, and at unceasing festivals the bards tuned their lutes and sang at the street corners.
29.nuance: The whole description is governed by the past-and-gone particle மன் (ஆடுமன், line 10) and by ஊங்கே, 'before', in the last line, so the poem is a portrait of a land as it was until the army came, not a picture of it now.

thinai_evidence.note: the enemy lands were happy only until the king's army spread over them

30.reading: The poet tells the fiercely angry king that his drum, roaring with a voice that shakes the earth like thunder, calls his never-retreating warriors to scatter the great rice, while the drum-rich kings and velir of every land, the sea shore of neythal, punnai, pearls and coral, the hills where hunters trade tusks and meat for liquor, the watered fields of sugarcane and festivals, the dry millet uplands and the sand-ridged forests, tremble though they hold forts in sea and forest; the rice ball raised by the priest for the god of the rite, a blood-soaked offering that the demoness shakes before and that even ants do not touch, is eaten by crows and kites.
30.nuance: Thirty lines survey every kind of land the enemies hold, sea, hill, field, upland and forest, so that the trembling of their kings at the drum (line 31) is the trembling of the whole land. The great rice is an offering before it is a meal: raised by the priest, shaken at by the demoness, left even by ants and eaten by crows and kites.

thinai_evidence.note: before the march, the king calls his warriors to the great rice offering

comparisons.tenor: the dark petals of the neythal

patikam:3.reading: The decade's preface says that Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan, younger brother of Imayavaramban, set his sceptre over Umbarkadu, struck down Agappa, performed sacrifice with the daytime fire, took to himself the elders of moon-clear tradition, divided and gave away land, led long rows of black elephants, bathed in the two seas in one day and worshipped Ayirai, and that, of unfailing fame and high learning, he went to the forest with Nedumbarathayanar going before him; Palai Gauthamanar sang the ten.
patikam:3.nuance: Only the preface tells that the king ended by leaving for the forest with a Brahmin teacher; the songs show him at war and at sacrifice. Agappa and Ayirai tie the preface to 22 and 21.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's conquests, gifts and final retreat to the forest

links.note: Kural 86 says the one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Patitruppattu 21 calls the king's kitchen-fat an ஆவுதி (oblation) beside the sacrificial one and says the two smells together please the gods who abide in the sky.
links.teaches: The Chera poem shows the mechanism the Kural only asserts: feeding guests reaches the gods because the kitchen smoke is itself counted as an oblation, so hospitality was understood as a second sacrifice rather than merely compared to one.

links.note: Kural 578 gives the world to those able to show kannottam without spoiling the task; Patitruppattu 22 lists கழிகண்ணோட்டம், excessive kindly regard, among the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, beside anger and harsh punishment.
links.teaches: The Chera list names as a fault exactly the excess the Kural's condition guards against, which shows that the Kural's praise of kannottam was already bounded in older court ethics where too much mercy blocked a king's justice.

links.note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's power; Patitruppattu 22 puts தெறல் கடுமை, severity of punishment, in one list with too much kindness and too much love as obstacles to dharma's wheel.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kural treats harshness on its own while the Chera poem sets it beside its opposite excesses, so the older list frames royal justice as a mean between cruelty and indulgence rather than as the avoidance of cruelty alone.

links.note: In Purananuru 23 the poet says he has come having seen Nedunchezhiyan's work in enemy land, which ends as a waste where a doe whose stag a tiger killed nibbles velai with her fawn; in Patitruppattu 23 the bards say they came and saw (கண்டனம்) the lands of the Chera's foes turned to forest where the wild cow lives happily with her bull.
links.teaches: The two bards' reports end on a female beast in the ruined land, but Kalladanar's widowed doe carries the human loss into the forest while Gauthamanar's paired wild cow celebrates the wilderness's return, so the same reporting convention could either mourn or exult over conquest.

links.note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; Patitruppattu 24 names the six duties (ஓதல் வேட்டல் அவைபிறர்ச் செய்தல் ஈதல் ஏற்றல்) and says the king walks by the word of those who keep them, so that the world walks by his.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the Brahmins' learning depend on the king's protection, while the Chera poem makes the king's conduct depend on the Brahmins' word, so the pair shows the relation running both ways: guarded by the king, they in turn guide him.

links.note: Kural 559 says if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain; Patitruppattu 24 ends that even if the rain-cloud forgets its season the king's wealth will keep its yield.
links.teaches: The Kural binds the land's rain to the king's justice, but the praise poem claims the just king's plenty survives even a failed monsoon, so court praise pushed royal power past the cosmic dependence the ethical maxim keeps.

links.note: Purananuru 25 asks whether Chezhiyan's spear stopped short of further ruin when he saw the widows beating their breasts and cutting their hair; in Patitruppattu 26 the poet himself says நோகோ யானே, I grieve, at the enemy land the Chera's warriors ravaged, whose people blame the season.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that pity for the conquered had a place inside victory praise in two forms, as the king's hoped-for restraint in the Pandya poem and as the poet's own grief in the Chera one, and in neither as blame of the king.

links.note: Patitruppattu 27 describes the enemy's watered land, ruined by the king's angry look, as knowing no uproar but the carters' shouting; 28 says the king's own land knows no heat but the uproar of the river's red flood.
links.teaches: The poet uses the same 'no uproar but a harmless one' figure for the land the king destroys and the land he guards, which shows that the two were equally blessed and that only the king's anger made the difference.

links.note: Purananuru 20 tells a Chera that those in his shade know no burning but the cooking fire and the sun, no bow but the rainbow and no weapon but the plough; Patitruppattu 28 says the Chera's land knows no heat but the uproar of the great river's flood, even in drought.
links.teaches: Both Chera poems praise the guarded land by negating violence with a harmless counterpart, and the Patitruppattu adds that the protection holds in drought because the river floods when the hills are dry, so the figure served as a court convention that each poet bent to a new claim.

links.note: Patitruppattu 23 shows the king feeding the street-singing bards (வயிரிய மாக்கள் ... மறுகுசிறை பாடும்) even in a drought; 29 uses the same line-words for bards tuning lutes and singing at street corners in the enemy's settlements before the army spread.
links.teaches: The singing bard is the decade's sign of a living land, so 29 measures the enemy's loss by the very figure 23 uses for the king's bounty: the war silences in other lands the music the king pays for at home.

links.note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan, called பெருஞ்சோற்று in his colophon name, for giving the great rice without limit while the hundred fought the five; Patitruppattu 30, colophon பெருஞ்சோற்றுநிலை, sung for a son of that line, shows the rite: the drum calls warriors to scatter the great rice, a blood-mixed ball offered to the god and eaten by crows and kites.
links.teaches: The father's poem only names the great rice as a gift of food, while the son's shows it as a pre-battle offering that binds the warriors and frightens the enemy, so the pair shows the perunjoru as a Chera rite of war that the Purananuru's epithet assumed.

links.note: Patitruppattu 24 praises the king for walking by the word of the Brahmins who keep the six duties; the preface of the decade says he made the elders of moon-clear tradition his own and finally went to the forest with Nedumbarathayanar leading.
links.teaches: The preface completes the portrait of 24: the king whose rule followed the learned Brahmins ended by following one of them out of rule into the forest, so the deference the song praises was remembered as leading to renunciation.

new_concepts.gloss: the great rice offered and shared before battle, binding warriors to the king
new_concepts.label_source: the text names it: பெருஞ்சோ(று) உகுத்தற்கு (30 line 43) and the colophon பெருஞ்சோற்றுநிலை

source_issues: 21-30: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai. 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29 and 30 are marked vanji here by their content (ravaged or threatened enemy land, the pre-battle rite); the colophons say paadaan forms except 30.
29: the colophon thurai is written without a space (வஞ்சித்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு), unlike 22, 23, 25 and 26.
22 line 22: வாயிதூங்குபு looks like வாயில் தூங்குபு run together with the ல் lost.
24 line 18: உண்மருந்(து) இன்மரும் is obscure; it probably stands for those who eat and those who chew (உண்மரும் தின்மரும்), and is marked uncertain.
28 line 6: நீணதொழில் is not a clear word and may be corrupt; marked uncertain.
30 line 21: செழும்பல் வைப்பி looks like வைப்பின் with the final ன் lost.
patikam:3 line 7: நீணரும் probably stands for நீரும் (இருகடல் நீரும், the waters of the two seas).
25 line 1: the repaired word (மாஆ டியபுலன்) comes from sangamtamil.com; lines 10-12 (the drum-bearing elephant and banners) are compressed and the reading is marked uncertain.

Repeated lines flagged: 23 line 10 = 43 line 11; 28 line 9 = 43 line 14; 30 line 40 = 34 line 2. 23 lines 5-6 and 29 lines 8-9 share the bards' line-words (வயிரிய மாக்கள், மறுகுசிறை பாடும்) without a flag.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 21 lines 27 and 34, 23 lines 7 and 21, 28 line 10, 30 line 6; the repaired readings are plausible.
